claim: Lier's Zimmertoren houses Louis Zimmer's astronomical Centenary Clock and the Astronomical Studio, a marquee combined-ticket Lier sight.
quote: The tower got its current name and function in the 1930s, when Belgian clockmaker and astronomer Louis Zimmer installed an astronomical clock in it.

claim: Lier's Begijnhof, founded 1258 with 11 streets and 162 houses, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1998.
quote: Founded in 1258, it has 11 streets and 162 houses, as well as a convent and an infirmary. In 1998 it was recognised as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.

claim: The Liers Vlaaike is a 300-year-old spiced regional pastry, recognised as a Flemish regional product (2007) and at EU level (2013).
quote: The Lier Vlaaike is a spicy pastry made with candy syrup and four spices that goes back more than 300 years and is one of the oldest regional pastries from the province of Antwerp.

claim: The Museum Wuyts-Van Campen & Baron Caroly in Lier was closed in February 2018, so it is no longer a planning option.
quote: At the end of February 2018, the Stedelijk Museum Wuyts-Van Campen & Baron Caroly was closed.

claim: Diest's Sint-Sulpitiuskerk (1320-1537) holds the tomb of Philip William of Orange-Nassau and a Religious Art museum in the choir.
quote: The monumental Sint-Sulpitiuskerk was built between 1320 and 1537 in local ironstone and white sandstone. For the main altar lies the tomb of Prince Philip William of Orange-Nassau, Lord of Diest.

claim: Diest's Groot Begijnhof, founded 1253, is UNESCO-listed and among the largest beguinages in the world.
quote: Diest is home to the Diest Beguinage, a tranquil complex founded in 1253 and recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Diest beguinage is one of the largest in the world.

claim: Diest's mid-19th-century citadel (1845-53) is described as the only European citadel where the defence system and architecture still survive intact.
quote: The citadel is the only citadel in Europe whose defence system and architecture still survive, with the main part built in 1845-53.

claim: Diest's only in-walls brewery is Loterbol, visitable on the first Saturday of the month - a small craft-beer draw rather than a major attraction.
quote: Diest has about 24,000 inhabitants and as far as I can see only one brewery and no distilleries within these old town ramparts. Loterbol is the only brewery, which you can visit on the first Saturday of the month.

claim: Turnhout's National Museum of the Playing Card showcases the city's heritage as one of the world's largest card producers (1.3 million packs/day), with antique printing machines on display.
quote: Turnhout was one of the world's largest producers of playing cards (1.3 million packs per day), and the museum displays a range of antique industrial printing machines used in card creation, including a vast steam-powered drive wheel.

claim: Turnhout's Kasteel van de Hertogen van Brabant dates from the 13th century but requires a 3-week-advance group booking and is not open to walk-in visitors.
quote: The castle is not open to the general public and requires a minimum of 3 weeks advance reservation as a group, and can only be visited under the guidance of a guide.

claim: Of the six candidate towns only Lier, Diest, and Turnhout sit on the 13-site UNESCO Flemish Beguinages list; Herentals, Aarschot, and Geel do not.
quote: Brugge, Dendermonde, Diest, Gent (Klein Begijnhof), Hoogstraten, Kortrijk, Leuven (Groot Begijnhof), Lier, Mechelen (Groot Begijnhof), Sint-Amandsberg, Sint-Truiden, Tongeren, Turnhout

claim: Herentals's original 13th-c. beguinage was destroyed in the Eighty Years' War; the present beguinage was rebuilt in the 17th century with a museum building open by appointment only.
quote: The original Begijnhof from the thirteenth century lay a small kilometer further north, but was destroyed during the Eighty Years' War. The current Begijnhof was built in the seventeenth century.

claim: Herentals's Sint-Catharinakerk in the beguinage is only freely visitable Fri-Sun 14:00-17:00 from 1 June to 30 September; outside that window guided tours only.
quote: The Sint-Catharinakerk in the Begijnhof can be visited from June 1 to September 30 on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays from 2 to 5 PM. Outside these hours, the church can only be visited with a guide.

claim: Geel's Sint-Dimpna church (begun 1349) and the Gasthuismuseum embody a unique medieval-rooted family-foster-care tradition still housing close to 500 psychiatric patients with townspeople today.
quote: A modern psychiatric centre now stands on the place of the old infirmary, with close to 500 patients still placed with inhabitants.

claim: Geel's Gasthuismuseum is housed in the former infirmary attached to Sint-Dimpnakerk and tells the story of medieval pilgrim care that evolved into the modern foster-family psychiatric model.
quote: An infirmary leans against the south side of the church's tower, where pilgrims who came seeking favor from the saint would find shelter for nine days.

claim: Aarschot's Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk is a gothic church built 1337-1450 in distinctive ironstone, damaged in both World Wars and restored 1971-87.
quote: This imposing gothic building was constructed between 1337 and 1450. The construction began in the early 14th century, with a foundation stone in the choir apse from 1337 mentioning French master builder Jacob Piccart.

claim: Aarschot's beguinage, founded ~1259, was largely destroyed in WWII; only the 17th-c. 'Zeven Weeën' row (nos. 15-19) remains intact, making it a ruin/fragment rather than a UNESCO-grade ensemble.
quote: During World War II, the courtyard was largely destroyed; only the section 'Zeven Weeën' (Beguinage numbers 15-19) was relatively well preserved, with 17th-century row houses featuring typical cross windows and distinctive rounded door openings.

claim: Lier's compact old town lets visitors walk between Zimmertoren, Begijnhof and Sint-Gummaruskerk in roughly 15 minutes, making it an efficient half-day cultural circuit.
quote: Most sights, from the Zimmertoren clock tower to the Beguinage, are within a 15-minute stroll.
